claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982; Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984.

claims.claim: Both DNA knots and catenanes can be created in vitro when high concentrations of eukaryotic topo II are present relative to DNA.
claims.source: Both DNA knots and catenanes can be created in vitro when high concentrations of eukaryotic topo II are present relative to DNA (Hsieh, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh, 1983.

claims.claim: The relative concentrations of both DNA and enzyme play a significant role in controlling whether type II topoisomerases selectively remove linkages or add linkages.
claims.source: Overall, the relative concentrations of both DNA and enzyme appear to play a significant role in controlling whether type II topoisomerases selectively remove linkages (simplifying DNA topology) or add linkages (complicating topology).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the preceding examples and citations.

claims.claim: Human topo II is present at low-to-sub micromolar levels in cells.
claims.source: In cells, DNA is maintained at a high concentration (millimolar base pairs) compared to that of the topoisomerase (e.g., human topo II is present at low-to-sub micromolar levels in cells [Padget et al., 2000]), yet the enzyme is capable of altering its catalytic output to suit specific needs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Padget et al., 2000.

claims.claim: During transcription and replication, positive DNA supercoils generated by RNA polymerases or replisomes are recognized and relaxed by type II topoisomerases to prevent stalling.
claims.source: For example, during transcription and replication, positive DNA supercoils generated by RNA polymerases or replisomes are recognized and relaxed by type II topoisomerases to prevent stalling (Liu and Wang, 1987; Lockshon and Morris, 1983; Pruss, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu and Wang, 1987; Lockshon and Morris, 1983; Pruss, 1985.

claims.claim: Following replication, interlinked chromosomes are decatenated by enzymes like topo II and topo IV to prevent DNA breaks.
claims.source: Similarly, following replication, interlinked chromosomes are decatenated by enzymes like topo II and topo IV to prevent DNA breaks (Cebrián et al., 2015; Hiasa and Marians, 1996; Lucas et al., 2001; Peter et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cebrián et al., 2015; Hiasa and Marians, 1996; Lucas et al., 2001; Peter et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Topo II can create knots in regions with high transcriptional activity.
claims.source: However, some type II topoisomerases can also create knots, such as the action of topo II in regions with high transcriptional activity (Valdés et al., 2018), a function that can locally compact DNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Valdés et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Topo II has been proposed to actively catenate DNA as a means of promoting chromosome condensation and/or cohesion.
claims.source: Topo II has also been proposed to actively catenate DNA as a means of promoting chromosome condensation and/or cohesion (Anderson and Roberge, 1996; Bauer et al., 2012; Farr et al., 2014; Ishida et al., 1994; Tavormina et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Roberge, 1996; Bauer et al., 2012; Farr et al., 2014; Ishida et al., 1994; Tavormina et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Vertebrates express two different topo II isoforms – Top2α and Top2β – that have specific cellular roles.
claims.source: One clue to understanding the disparate topological outcomes mediated by type II topoisomerases can be found in vertebrates, which express two different topo II isoforms – Top2α and Top2β – that have specific cellular roles.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate topo II isoforms.

claims.claim: Top2α is essential in dividing cells where it assists in cell-cycle functions such as chromosome condensation and segregation.
claims.source: Top2α is essential in dividing cells where it assists in cell-cycle functions such as chromosome condensation and segregation (Gonzalez et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2020; Samejima et al., 2012; Spence et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Gonzalez et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2020; Samejima et al., 2012; Spence et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Top2β plays a role in supporting transcriptional initiation.
claims.source: By comparison, Top2β plays a role in supporting transcriptional initiation (Edmond et al., 2017; Haffner et al., 2010; Lyu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Edmond et al., 2017; Haffner et al., 2010; Lyu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Functional differences between Top2α and Top2β derive in part from a variable, intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) appended to an evolutionarily conserved catalytic core.
claims.source: Evidence suggests that functional differences between Top2α and Top2β derive in part from a variable, intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) appended to an evolutionarily conserved catalytic core (Linka et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Linka et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The CTD of topo II is subject to extensive post-translational modifications.
claims.source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The CTD has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins.
claims.source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997.

claims.claim: The CTD of Top2α appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres.
claims.source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Some proteins known to associate with topo IIs and some genetic loci where the enzyme is enriched have been proposed to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
claims.source: Interestingly, some proteins known to associate with topo IIs and some genetic loci where the enzyme is enriched have been proposed to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming assemblies that distinguish them from general chromatin areas (Boija et al., 2018; Cebrián et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018; Frattini et al., 2021; Trivedi et al., 2019; Yamane et al., 1997; Zamudio et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Boija et al., 2018; Cebrián et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018; Frattini et al., 2021; Trivedi et al., 2019; Yamane et al., 1997; Zamudio et al., 2019.

claims.claim: During LLPS, macromolecules locally concentrate to form a new fluid phase that demixes from the bulk solution to establish a dynamic, membraneless compartment.
claims.source: During LLPS, macromolecules locally concentrate to form a new fluid phase that demixes from the bulk solution to establish a dynamic, membraneless compartment (Banani et al., 2017; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017.

claims.claim: The CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
claims.source: Limited proteolysis studies (Austin et al., 1995), as well as primary sequence analysis using the disordered protein prediction algorithm IUPRed2A (Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020), indicate that the CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Austin et al., 1995 and Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020, and by disorder prediction data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: IDRs have been shown to facilitate the self-assembly of macromolecules into liquid-like condensates through phase separation in a variety of protein systems.
claims.source: IDRs have been shown to facilitate the self-assembly of macromolecules into liquid-like condensates through phase separation in a variety of protein systems (Banani et al., 2017; Lyon et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Lyon et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity.
claims.source: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity (Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017); exceptions include factors that support the initiation of DNA replication in metazoans, which have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues (Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019), and the Nephrin Intracellular Domain (NICD) (Pak et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic replication initiators have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues.
claims.source: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity (Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017); exceptions include factors that support the initiation of DNA replication in metazoans, which have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues (Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019), and the Nephrin Intracellular Domain (NICD) (Pak et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Topo II CTDs generally have a high lysine content (≥15%), a moderately high amount of serine (~10%), aspartate, and glutamate (10%), and a very low percentage of each aromatic amino acid (<5%).
claims.source: Analysis of the relative amino-acid composition of topo II CTDs shows that despite having relatively sparse sequence homology to each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the elements generally have a high lysine content (≥15%), a moderately high amount of serine (~10%), aspartate, and glutamate (10%), and a very low percentage of each aromatic amino acid (<5%) (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on amino acid composition analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic topo II CTDs can have different compositions of positively and negatively charged amino acids and varied isoelectric points (pI = 5.5–9.6).
claims.source: Despite these similarities, eukaryotic topo II CTDs can have different compositions of positively and negatively charged amino acids and varied isoelectric points (pI = 5.5–9.6) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The compositional properties of the topo II CTDs are more similar to those of the eukaryotic replication initiators, as opposed to low-complexity sequences found in representative LLPS-forming proteins such as human FUS or DDX4.
claims.source: Overall, the compositional properties of the topo II CTDs are more similar to those of the eukaryotic replication initiators, as opposed to low-complexity sequences found in representative LLPS-forming proteins such as human FUS (Wang et al., 2018a) or DDX4 (Nott et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to Wang et al., 2018a and Nott et al., 2015.

claims.claim: At the lowest concentration of ScTop2 tested (50nM), no visible bodies were seen.
claims.source: At the lowest concentration of ScTop2 tested (50nM), no visible bodies were seen.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At moderate protein concentrations (375nM), small circular fluorescent bodies became apparent.
claims.source: However, at moderate protein concentrations (375nM), small circular fluorescent bodies became apparent.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Puncta formed by ScTop2 grew in size and number as protein concentration increased.
claims.source: These bodies (referred to hereafter as 'puncta') grew in size and number as protein concentration increased.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The formation of puncta by ScTop2 was time-dependent, with puncta appearing within 10min of mixing and plateauing in number and size after~60min.
claims.source: While conducting these experiments, we noted that the formation of puncta was time-dependent, with puncta appearing within 10min of mixing and plateauing in number and size after~60min (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Both ScTop2 protein and DNA co-localize in the puncta.
claims.source: Imaging at Cy3 and Cy5 excitation wavelengths showed that both protein and DNA co-localize in the puncta; the labeled DNA on its own did not form such bodies (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on dual-channel confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: DNA-dependent stimulation of puncta formation was also observed when Cy3-ScTop2 was mixed with an unlabeled negatively supercoiled 2.9kb plasmid (pSG483).
claims.source: DNA-dependent stimulation of puncta formation was also observed when Cy3-ScTop2 was mixed with an unlabeled negatively supercoiled 2.9kb plasmid (pSG483) (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Puncta formed in the presence of DNA were noticeably larger compared to those formed without.
claims.source: Interestingly, puncta formed in the presence of DNA were noticeably larger compared to those formed without (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM and that DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into these bodies.
claims.evidence: This is based on the confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into ScTop2 bodies.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM and that DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into these bodies.
claims.evidence: This is based on the confocal microscopy data presented in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: The shortest DNA tested (50bp) did not increase the number nor the size of condensates at any concentration tested.
claims.source: The shortest DNA tested (50bp, roughly the binding site size of the catalytic region) did not increase the number nor the size of condensates at any concentration tested.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The 100bp, 200bp, and pSG483 DNA substrates all enhanced condensate formation at intermediate mass concentrations (5–20ng/µL).
claims.source: By comparison, the 100bp, 200bp, and pSG483 DNA substrates all enhanced condensate formation at intermediate mass concentrations (5–20ng/µL).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Heparin failed to stimulate DNA condensation at the observed concentrations.
claims.source: To determine whether the stimulation of condensation was dependent on DNA, a titration was also conducted with another polyanionic substrate, heparin. Interestingly, heparin failed to stimulate DNA condensation at the observed concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Condensate formation by ScTop2 is aided by extended DNA segments and is not stimulated simply by the presence of a poly-anionic substrate.
claims.source: Together, these findings establish that condensate formation by ScTop2 is aided by extended DNA segments and is not stimulated simply by the presence of a poly-anionic substrate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the DNA length and heparin titration experiments.

claims.claim: Nucleic-acid binding proteins that undergo phase separation tend to exhibit a biphasic response with respect to the relative concentration of DNA or RNA.
claims.source: Nucleic-acid binding proteins that undergo phase separation tend to exhibit a biphasic response with respect to the relative concentration of DNA or RNA (Du and Chen, 2018; Maharana et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015): as a nucleic acid substrate is titrated against a fixed amount of protein, condensation is first promoted, but then as concentrations are increased further, the protein is solubilized and condensation is antagonized.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Du and Chen, 2018; Maharana et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015.

claims.claim: At low DNA concentrations (5–10nM), the number and size of puncta increased relative to samples in the absence of DNA.
claims.source: At low DNA concentrations (5–10nM), the number and size of puncta increased relative to samples in the absence of DNA.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: As the DNA concentration was increased further, puncta disappeared.
claims.source: By contrast, as the DNA concentration was increased further, puncta disappeared.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate.
claims.source: Interestingly, at the intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate (Figure 2E); by comparison, puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
claims.source: Interestingly, at the intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate (Figure 2E); by comparison, puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations.

claims.claim: This size-dependent type of behavior has been previously seen with other DNA-binding proteins that undergo LLPS, such as HP1α.
claims.source: This size-dependent type of behavior has been previously seen with other DNA-binding proteins that undergo LLPS, such as HP1α (Keenen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Keenen et al., 2021.

claims.claim: In reactions lacking DNA, the intensity of the Cy3-ScTop2 puncta did not recover following photobleaching, suggesting that these bodies possess more gel-like characteristics.
claims.source: In reactions lacking DNA, the intensity of the Cy3-ScTop2 puncta did not recover following photobleaching, suggesting that these bodies possess more gel-like characteristics (Frey et al., 2006; Jawerth et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Frey et al., 2006; Jawerth et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In the presence of 5nM unlabeled pSG483, a fraction of the Cy3-ScTop2 intensity (roughly one-third) had recovered by the 15 minute mark.
claims.source: By contrast, in the presence of 5nM unlabeled pSG483, a fraction of the Cy3-ScTop2 intensity (roughly one-third) had recovered by the same 15minute mark.
claims.evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: As the pSG483 concentration increased, the mobile protein fraction inside the puncta appeared to decrease.
claims.source: As the pSG483 concentration increased, the mobile protein fraction inside the puncta appeared to decrease, with the fibrillar bodies (25–50nM DNA) showing somewhat less fluidity than the spherical droplets (5–10nM DNA).
claims.evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Time-lapse microscopy of puncta containing ScTop2 and 5nM pSG483 revealed fusion events between puncta on the order of minutes.
claims.source: Time-lapse microscopy of puncta containing ScTop2 and 5nM pSG483 also revealed fusion events between puncta on the order of minutes (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: While the smaller puncta formed by ScTop2 on its own are relatively static, the protein in both the spherical and fibrillar structures formed by ScTop2 in the presence of DNA is dynamic, exhibiting the defining attributes of condensates formed by LLPS.
claims.source: Thus, while the smaller puncta formed by ScTop2 on its own are relatively static, the protein in both the spherical and fibrillar structures formed by ScTop2 in the presence of DNA is dynamic, exhibiting the defining attributes of condensates formed by LLPS.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP and fusion data.

claims.claim: The Cy3-ScTop2ΔCTD construct did not form condensates in either the presence or absence of a 200bp Cy5-labeled DNA, even at protein concentrations as high as 1μM.
claims.source: The Cy3-ScTop2ΔCTD construct did not form condensates in either the presence or absence of a 200bp Cy5-labeled DNA, even at protein concentrations as high as 1μM.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The Cy3-labeled CTD failed to form condensates in the absence of DNA but did form bodies in the presence of 50nM Cy5-labeled 200bp duplex at a lower salt concentration of 50mM KOAc.
claims.source: By comparison, the Cy3-labeled CTD failed to form condensates in the absence of DNA but did form bodies in the presence of 50nM Cy5-labeled 200bp duplex at a lower salt concentration of 50mM KOAc (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Several puncta formed with the CTD alone integrated DNA into only a portion of the bodies, as compared to the fully homogenous distribution of DNA seen with full-length ScTop2.
claims.source: Interestingly, several puncta formed with the CTD alone integrated DNA into only a portion of the bodies, as compared to the fully homogenous distribution of DNA seen with full-length ScTop2 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The addition of PEG as a crowding agent induced puncta formation by the CTD, but in a manner that did not require DNA.
claims.source: The addition of PEG as a crowding agent also induced puncta formation by the CTD, but in a manner that did not require DNA, indicating that this region can weakly associate with itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme.
claims.source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that the ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme and that DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the element.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the deletion and isolated CTD experiments.

claims.claim: DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the CTD element.
claims.source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that the ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme and that DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the element.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the CTD experiments with DNA.

claims.claim: In the absence of DNA, the small puncta formed by ScTop2 alone at the control potassium acetate concentration (150mM) disappeared as soon as salt levels were increased to 200mM.
claims.source: In the absence of DNA, the small puncta formed by ScTop2 alone at the control potassium acetate concentration (150mM) disappeared as soon as salt levels were increased to 200mM.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In the presence of pSG483, the large condensates seen at 150mM salt persisted until potassium acetate levels reached 400mM.
claims.source: By comparison, in the presence of pSG483, the large condensates seen at 150mM salt persisted until potassium acetate levels reached 400mM.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The intermediate salt concentrations still supported solubilization of ScTop2 condensates by elevated levels of plasmid DNA.
claims.source: Interestingly, the intermediate salt concentrations still supported solubilization of ScTop2 condensates by elevated levels of plasmid DNA.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 1,6-hexanediol strongly promoted the aggregation of ScTop2 into large, irregular bodies in both the presence and absence of DNA while also preventing the resolubilization of the bodies when pSG483 concentrations were increased.
claims.source: Interestingly, 1,6-HD strongly promoted the aggregation of ScTop2 into large, irregular bodies in both the presence and absence of DNA while also preventing the resolubilization of the bodies when pSG483 concentrations were increased.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The addition of higher levels of 1,6-HD (e.g. 10%) severely disrupted DNA supercoil relaxation by ScTop2.
claims.source: The addition of higher levels of 1,6-HD (e.g. 10%) also severely disrupted DNA supercoil relaxation by ScTop2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that the agent has a detrimental effect on the protein.
claims.evidence: This is based on activity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The CTD was unable to form condensates in the absence of DNA, even when the salt concentration was lowered to 50mM potassium acetate.
claims.source: As seen previously, the CTD was unable to form condensates in the absence of DNA, even when the salt concentration was lowered to 50mM potassium acetate (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Robust CTD-DNA interactions were seen at 50mM salt concentration, as evidenced by the presence of large numbers of large puncta and by the co-localization of DNA inside the CTD bodies.
claims.source: However, robust CTD-DNA interactions were seen at this lower salt concentration, as evidenced not only by the presence of large numbers of large puncta, but also by the co-localization of DNA inside the CTD bodies; as salt concentration was increased, puncta became more diffuse.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: As salt concentration was increased, puncta formed by the CTD became more diffuse.
claims.source: However, robust CTD-DNA interactions were seen at this lower salt concentration, as evidenced not only by the presence of large numbers of large puncta, but also by the co-localization of DNA inside the CTD bodies; as salt concentration was increased, puncta became more diffuse.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 1,6-hexanediol had little effect on condensate formation by the CTD.
claims.source: By comparison, 1,6-hexanediol had little effect on condensate formation by the CTD.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Condensate formation by ScTop2 is primarily reliant on ionic protein-DNA interactions and not on contacts involving aromatic amino acids.
claims.source: Overall, our data indicate that condensate formation by ScTop2 is primarily reliant on ionic protein-DNA interactions and, consistent with its Tyr-, Phe-, and Trp-poor amino acid composition (Figure 2B), not on contacts involving aromatic amino acids.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the salt and 1,6-hexanediol experiments and the amino acid composition data.

claims.claim: The propensity of IDRs to form condensates can be fine-tuned by post-translational modifications.
claims.source: The propensity of IDRs to form condensates can be fine-tuned by post-translational modifications (Larson et al., 2017; Nott et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018b; Wang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Larson et al., 2017; Nott et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018b; Wang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Topo II CTDs are modified by phosphorylation.
claims.source: Since topo II CTDs are modified by phosphorylation (Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992), we asked whether phosphorylation status might impact the enzyme's ability to undergo LLPS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992.

claims.claim: In the absence of DNA, the phosphatase-treated and untreated (control) enzymes both had the same condensate-forming propensity.
claims.source: In the absence of DNA, the phosphatase-treated and untreated (control) enzymes both had the same condensate-forming propensity.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: As pSG483 was first added (5nM), phosphatase treated ScTop2 produced a larger number of small puncta as compared to the smaller number of large droplets formed with the control reaction.
claims.source: However, as pSG483 was first added (5nM), phosphatase treated ScTop2 produced a larger number of small puncta as compared to the smaller number of large droplets formed with the control reaction (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: As pSG483 concentration was further increased (25nM), the phosphatase-treated sample produced more elongated fibrillar bodies than the control.
claims.source: As pSG483 concentration was further increased (25nM), the phosphatase-treated sample produced more elongated fibrillar bodies than the control.
claims.evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry analysis confirmed that the phosphatase stripped phosphates off from all amino acids in the CTD.
claims.source: Mass spectrometry analysis confirmed that the phosphatase stripped phosphates off from all amino acids in the CTD (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Phosphatase-treated protein produced assemblies that failed to recover fluorescence intensity in the absence of DNA.
claims.source: Similarly to the native phosphorylated samples, phosphatase- treated protein produced assemblies that failed to recover fluorescence intensity in the absence of DNA (Figure 4F).

results.result: Budding yeast topo II (ScTop2) forms higher-order spherical assemblies (puncta) at physiological protein concentrations (>250 nM), with puncta size and number increasing with protein concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C38-C40, and C45 are supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2C showing concentration-dependent puncta formation. The observations are consistent across multiple protein concentrations and the physiological relevance is established by comparison to reported cellular concentrations.

results.result: DNA stimulates condensation of ScTop2 and is integrated into the puncta. DNA exhibits a biphasic effect: low concentrations (5-10 nM) increase puncta size and number, while higher concentrations (>50 nM) cause resolubilization. Plasmid DNA forms elongated fibrillar structures at intermediate concentrations, while short DNAs remain spherical.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C42-C44, C46, and C52-C55 are supported by dual-channel confocal microscopy (Figure 2D-E, Figure 3A) showing DNA colocalization and biphasic concentration dependence. The morphological differences between plasmid and short DNA substrates are documented in Figure 2E.

results.result: Condensate formation by ScTop2 requires extended DNA segments (≥100 bp) and is not stimulated by polyanionic substrates like heparin, indicating specificity for DNA rather than general polyanion binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by DNA length titration experiments (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showing that 50 bp DNA does not enhance condensation while 100 bp, 200 bp, and plasmid DNA do. The heparin control (C49) demonstrates specificity for DNA.

results.result: ScTop2 puncta exhibit liquid-like properties in the presence of DNA. Without DNA, puncta are gel-like (no FRAP recovery), but with 5 nM DNA, approximately one-third of protein recovers within 15 minutes. Puncta also undergo fusion events on the order of minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by FRAP experiments (Figure 3B) showing DNA-dependent fluidity and time-lapse microscopy (Figure 3C) demonstrating fusion events. The distinction between gel-like (no DNA) and liquid-like (with DNA) behavior is clearly documented.

results.result: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of ScTop2 is necessary for LLPS. Deletion of the CTD (ScTop2ΔCTD) prevents condensate formation even at high protein concentrations (1 μM) and in the presence of DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C62, and C66 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 4A) showing that ScTop2ΔCTD does not form condensates under conditions where full-length protein does. This establishes the CTD as necessary for LLPS.

results.result: The isolated ScTop2 CTD cannot form condensates alone but does so in the presence of DNA (at 50 mM KOAc) or crowding agents like PEG. DNA acts as a scaffold to promote CTD co-localization, though DNA integration is less homogeneous than with full-length protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C67, and C123 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing CTD condensation requires DNA or PEG. The partial DNA integration (C64) is documented in Figure 4A.

results.result: ScTop2 condensation is primarily driven by ionic protein-DNA interactions. Salt titration shows that DNA-free puncta dissolve at 200 mM KOAc, while DNA-containing condensates persist until 400 mM KOAc. Intermediate salt concentrations still support DNA-mediated resolubilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 and C77 are supported by salt titration experiments (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing differential salt sensitivity. The conclusion about ionic interactions (C77) is further supported by the amino acid composition data (Figure 2B) and 1,6-hexanediol experiments.

results.result: 1,6-hexanediol promotes aggregation of ScTop2 into large irregular bodies and prevents DNA-mediated resolubilization, but has little effect on the isolated CTD. High concentrations (10%) disrupt ScTop2 enzymatic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C72, and C76 are supported by confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The differential effect on full-length vs. CTD suggests the catalytic core is affected by 1,6-HD.

results.result: Phosphorylation status of ScTop2 does not control LLPS ability but modulates condensate physical properties. Phosphatase-treated ScTop2 forms more numerous small puncta at low DNA concentrations and more fibrillar bodies at intermediate DNA concentrations. Critically, dephosphorylation eliminates DNA-induced fluidity in FRAP experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), mass spectrometry (Figure 4D), and FRAP data (Figure 4E-F). The mass spec confirms complete dephosphorylation of CTD residues, and FRAP shows loss of DNA-induced mobility.

results.result: Condensation induces ScTop2 to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation. At 150 mM KOAc and 100 nM ScTop2 (no condensates), ~80% supercoil relaxation occurs. At higher protein concentrations where condensates form, DNA converts to well-shifted catenated products. At 400 mM KOAc (no condensates), only relaxed topoisomers are observed. The catenated products can be decatenated by dissolving condensates with high salt.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C88-C93, and C140 are supported by combined confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 5A-B) showing correlation between condensate formation and catenation. The restriction enzyme experiments (Figure 5B) confirm the well-shifted species are catenanes that can be decatenated by salt-induced condensate dissolution.

results.result: Deletion of the ScTop2 CTD shifts enzymatic activity from catenation to robust DNA knotting. ScTop2ΔCTD shows nearly complete supercoil relaxation at 100 nM, but at higher concentrations (250-1000 nM) produces extensive DNA knotting as evidenced by ladder patterns on gels after nicking. The catalytic core is highly efficient at forming DNA knots at physiological enzyme concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C94-C98, C100, and C142 are supported by activity assays with nicking experiments (Figure 5C-D) showing characteristic knot ladder patterns. The interpretation is supported by citations to prior work on DNA knotting and comparison to Figure 1.

results.result: Full-length ScTop2 also forms knots, but catenanes are the principal product when condensation occurs. The CTD routes knotting activity into robust catenane production.
results.evaluation: Claims C99 and C101 are supported by nicking experiments with full-length ScTop2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) showing that while knots are present, catenanes predominate under condensate-forming conditions. This contrasts with the CTD-deleted enzyme.

results.result: Human TOP2α and TOP2β can form condensates with DNA. TOP2α weakly forms bodies alone at 1 μM but shows marked increase with 50 nM DNA. TOP2β produces larger puncta alone and is only moderately enhanced by DNA. DNA colocalizes with both proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C108 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 6A) showing differential condensation behavior between the two human isoforms and DNA colocalization in both cases.

results.result: TOP2α and TOP2β have different condensate-forming potentials. TOP2α shows limited puncta formation alone (≤3 μm² at 1 μM) but strong DNA-dependent enhancement. TOP2β forms larger bodies at lower concentrations (50-100 nM) that exceed DNA-free ScTop2 size. Both show biphasic DNA response with stimulation at low-moderate concentrations and resolubilization at high concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C114 are supported by systematic concentration titrations (Figure 6B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing quantitative differences in condensation behavior between isoforms while maintaining qualitative similarity in DNA response.

results.result: The ability to couple catenation to condensation is conserved across eukaryotic topo IIs. TOP2α shows supercoil relaxation at 100 nM but switches to catenation at ≥250 nM when puncta appear. TOP2β shows similar behavior at slightly lower concentrations (250 nM), consistent with enhanced condensation properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 and C141 are supported by combined confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 6D-E) showing correlation between condensate formation and catenation for both human isoforms, paralleling the ScTop2 results.

results.result: The CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) with characteristic amino acid composition: high lysine (≥15%), moderate serine (~10%), aspartate and glutamate (10%), and very low aromatic content (<5%). Despite varied isoelectric points (pI 5.5-9.6), their composition is more similar to eukaryotic replication initiators than to typical low-complexity LLPS proteins like FUS or DDX4.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C35-C37 are supported by disorder prediction analysis (Figure 2A) and amino acid composition analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The comparative analysis with other LLPS proteins is documented.

results.result: Puncta formation by ScTop2 is time-dependent, appearing within 10 minutes and plateauing in number and size after ~60 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by time-lapse microscopy data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) showing kinetics of puncta formation.

results.result: The isolated CTD requires lower salt (50 mM KOAc) to form condensates with DNA, showing robust CTD-DNA interactions evidenced by large puncta and DNA colocalization. Higher salt concentrations make puncta more diffuse.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C124 are supported by salt titration experiments with isolated CTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing salt-dependent condensation behavior.

results.result: Full-length ScTop2 forms condensed bodies in the absence of DNA at physiological salt (150 mM KOAc) and protein concentrations (0.5-1.5 μM). These DNA-free assemblies are gel-like (no FRAP recovery) but dissolve at ≥200 mM KOAc, demonstrating they are not irreversible aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 2C), FRAP data (Figure 3B), and salt titration (Figure 4B). The physiological relevance is established by citation to cellular concentrations.

results.result: The difference in salt and DNA sensitivities between isolated CTD and full-length enzyme is likely due to additional DNA contacts through the cleavage core (20-30 bp binding) and ATPase region. Since ≥100 bp DNA is needed for LLPS, DNA likely acts as a bridge. Multiple protein-DNA contacts and CTD-CTD interactions facilitate phase separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by the DNA length requirement data (Figure 2E) and are consistent with structural knowledge of topo II DNA binding (supported by citations). The inference about bridging is reasonable given the data.

results.result: ScTop2 and TOP2α show closely matched LLPS response with strong DNA dependency, while TOP2β more readily forms condensates alone and is less influenced by DNA at higher concentrations. This difference may be attributable to isoelectric points: basic for ScTop2 and TOP2α, acidic for TOP2β.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C174 are supported by comparative confocal microscopy data and amino acid composition analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 6). The correlation with pI is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: A mechanistic model for knotting: The sharp DNA bend introduced by the cleavage core contributes to knot formation. At low protein concentrations, enzymes preferentially resolve pre-existing crossovers (e.g., supercoils). As protein concentration increases, more DNA bends lead to compaction and increased likelihood of crossovers forming between segments of the same plasmid, which when acted upon by topo II generate knots. The density of knot crossovers should be proportional to plasmid compaction, which depends on local topo II:DNA ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C151 present a mechanistic model supported by the knotting data (Figure 5D), structural knowledge (citations to Dong and Berger, 2007; Vologodskii et al., 2001), and comparison to prior work (Hsieh, 1983; Wasserman and Cozzarelli, 1991). The model is consistent with the experimental observations.

results.result: A mechanistic model for catenation: The CTD creates bridges between plasmid molecules that locally concentrate DNA and topo II, facilitating crossover formation between different DNA molecules leading to catenanes. CTD-less ScTop2 forms some catenanes at intermediate concentrations (250-500 nM) but only knots at 1000 nM. As protein concentration increases, strand passage in cis (knots) outcompetes passage in trans (catenanes) unless the CTD is present to favor inter-DNA links. At intermediate concentrations, mixtures of products reflect equilibrium between local enzyme/DNA concentration and access to cis vs. trans crossovers.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 present a mechanistic model supported by the comparative activity data for full-length vs. CTD-deleted enzyme (Figure 5C-D, Figure 7C-D). The model explains the observed product distributions and is consistent with the LLPS data.

results.result: Both knotting and catenation, but not supercoil relaxation, are abolished by high salt (400 mM). Elevated ionic strength prevents CTD-facilitated LLPS and weakens DNA-catalytic core interactions, antagonizing loop formation and shifting activity toward resolving pre-existing crossovers.
results.evaluation: Claim C159 is supported by activity assays at different salt concentrations (Figure 4B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing selective abolition of knotting and catenation while relaxation persists.
